by Rick McGinnis Rick's Flicks August 29, 2026 at 12:08 pm https://www.steynonline.com/16381/ladies-first-joe-mankiewicz-a-letter-to-three  Joe Manckiewicz' A Letter to Three Wives was released in 1949, four years after the end of World War Two, twenty after the stock market crash, and a year before the '50s began and – at least in the eyes of social history – America was fully in the throes of the postwar economic miracle. It's one of those films whose story, compelling on its own, is thick with signs and artifacts of the time when it was released. The same film, made five years later, would have looked and felt very different. To set the scene, 1949 was the year of the first TV western, Hopalong Cassidy, and the first Emmy Awards. It saw Death of a Salesman and South Pacific open on Broadway and Laurence Olivier's Hamlet won the Academy Awards. It was the year when NATO was founded, and of the Revolt of the Admirals. Glenn Dunaway won the first NASCAR race, U.S. troops left South Korea, President Harry Truman started his first full term and inaugurated the Fair Deal program and the first Volkswagen Beetle arrived in the United States. There were a few significant deaths: actor Wallace Beery, Gone with the Wind director Victor Fleming and author Margaret Mitchell, philanthropist Solomon R. Guggenheim, the blues musician Huddie "Leadbelly" Ledbetter and publisher Nelson Doubleday. But the list of births is a barrage of Boomer icons: John Belushi, Jessica Lange, Billy Joel, Lionel Richie, Shelley Duvall, Keith Carradine, Manson family member Leslie Van Houten, Richard Gere, Bruce Springsteen, Annie Liebovitz, Jeff Bridges, Sissy Spacek, Meryl Streep and all of the original lineup of ZZ Top. The film begins with a tour of its locale, conducted by a character who we hear about constantly but never see. Addie Ross is the picture's narrator, voiced by Celeste Holm, and she introduces the character and the nameless town they live in: a suburb – what we would come to call a "bedroom community" – half an hour from a major city by train (slightly less if you catch the express). The town is an American microcosm, stratified into neat class layers, starting on the affluent, old money street where Deborah Bishop (Jeanne Crain) lives with her husband Brad (Jeffrey Lynn), who built the house before he enlisted in the navy and brought the WAVES officer he married home. The next stop is the adjacent middle-class neighbourhood where, as Addie states, you live when you're on your way up or down. It's here we're introduced to Rita Phipps (Ann Sothern) and her husband George (Kirk Douglas) who are, Addie tells us, definitely on their way up. He's a high school teacher; she writes for the radio and makes more money than he does. Deborah and Rita do the sort of charity work women in their social position did not so long ago, along with a third friend, Lora Mae (Linda Darnell), who's married to Porter Hollingsway (Paul Douglas), a department store mogul.   All three women are friends with – or rather are obliged to live in close social proximity to – the unseen Addie, more because of their husbands than through any choice of their own. Once married to a man she jettisoned long before the story begins, Addie is a sore spot in their lives – an ideal they can't live up to; a woman with qualities they fear they lack. And she has apparently just quit town, subletting her house and selling her car a week before the three women meet up to escort a boat load of underprivileged children on an outing in the country. Just as the boat is about to leave a special delivery postman – was there ever such a thing outside of the movies? – arrives on his bicycle and hands them a letter from Addie. After a preamble laced with the kind of acid sweetness it's hard to imagine from a man, she informs her three dear friends that she has indeed left town with a souvenir – one of their husbands. The three women try to remain calm as they silently stare at the telephone booth on the dock while the boat pulls away. What follows is a kind of murder mystery without a body – a "whodunnit" about infidelity that will be answered in the last minutes of the picture.   A Letter to Three Wives is based on Letter to Five Wives, a novel by John Klempner that ran in a 1946 issue of Cosmopolitan – a property that had stumped a series of writers under contract to 20th Century Fox, including Joe Manckiewicz. Vera Caspary – the author of the novel Laura – took it on and eliminated one of the five couples in Klempner's story and moved the narrator offscreen. Mankiewicz was desperate to write and direct it as his next picture, but Daryl F. Zanuck at Fox had no intention of giving him the job, offering it to Ernst Lubitsch, who was in poor health. Producer Sol Siegel persuaded Zanuck to change his mind but when Mankiewicz failed to turn in a promised new draft of the script while in England working on the thriller Escape, Zanuck wrote him a scolding letter listing every way that Mankiewicz had failed him so far. "In view of what appears to be a pretty disheartening financial record, I must be considered a rather expensive luxury at the present time," Mankiewicz wrote back, striving mightily to feign humility. "Merely to point out that my last two films cost too much money and were box-office flops, doesn't necessarily mean that I am an expensive director. It may mean that I am a bad director – which is always a frightening possibility."   Somewhere between this letter and the start of production the film lost another wife, and Zanuck was forced to admit to Siegel that Mankiewicz' finished script was "magnificent, one of the best scripts of its type I have ever read. It looks like at long last Mr. Mankiewicz is going to be associated with a very big picture." The first of a series of flashbacks tells the story of Deborah and Brad beginning just after their wedding, when he brings the former farm girl home to his mansion and introduces her to his friends at the annual spring country club dance. She's nervous and takes too many of the martinis he offers her and confides in Rita how out of place she feels in her new life, with only an old, out-of-fashion dress to wear to her introduction to Brad's friends. Rita offers both comforting words and a last-minute alteration to the dress, but it all goes wrong in a mildly slapstick scene at the dance where Deborah embarrasses herself while learning about Addie, Brad's former fiancée. It's hard to like Deborah, harder to like Brad. She's insecure and brittle, suspicious of a husband she considers above her station and jealous of the hovering threat of Addie Ross. He's careless, thoughtless and entitled, blandly charming but oblivious to his wife's ongoing distress and the least interesting character in the picture.   Crain was one of those actors who never developed a distinct screen persona, and her career was something like a "utility actress", filling parts that most stars and starlets would consider lacking glamour. She wasn't without talent – she could play the luckless sister to Gene Tierney's sociopath in Leave Her to Heaven, the oldest daughter of Clifton Webb and Myrna Loy's vast brood in Cheaper by the Dozen, the restless country girl in State Fair and half of a sister act opposite Jane Russell in Gentlemen Marry Brunettes. Rita and George Phipps are a far more appealing couple, in spite of their problems. Sothern's Rita is the emotional heart of the group, both ambitious and empathetic, a mother and a career woman. Thanks to her popular Maisie films at MGM – which saw a hit spin-off on the radio – Sothern was probably the biggest star in the cast, on loan to Fox for the picture. Kirk Douglas, by contrast, was a relative newcomer with only a half dozen films to his credit, the best of which was Out of the Past.   Rita's flashback is a disastrous dinner party she held for her imperious boss, Mrs. Manleigh (Florence Bates) and her desiccated husband (Hobart Cavanagh). She realizes, too late in the day, that while anxiously preparing for the evening she's forgotten her husband's birthday when Addie Ross sends him a thoughtful gift. The dinner is a disaster, partly because the Manleighs are insufferable bores straight out of Sinclair Lewis' Babbitt, partly because she's striving to make an impression on her unworthy guests. But the party brings out the less attractive side of George, who already carries a chip on his shoulder about being an underpaid and overeducated high school teacher. "I'm willing to admit that to a majority of my fellow citizens I'm a slightly comic figure: an educated man," he tells his wife after their guests have left. "I'm a schoolteacher. That's even worse than being an intellectual. Schoolteachers are not only comic they're often cold and hungry in this richest land on earth." But the party reveals George's pedantic side when he insists on playing the whole of his gift from Addie Ross – a 78rpm album of a Brahms concerto – to their disinterested guests, who respond in kind by making everyone sit through a horrid and interminable soap opera on the radio. This prompts a dyspeptic rant from George about the crass, blaring, tasteless medium, then at its commercial and cultural apogee.   "None of that bilge has the remotest connection with good writing," he seethes at Mrs. Manleigh, his pipe gripped in his fist "The purpose of radio writing as far as I can see is to prove that a deodorant can bring happiness, a mouthwash guarantees success and a laxative attracts romance. Don't think, said the radio, and we'll pay you for it. Can't spell 'cat'? Too bad, but a yacht and a million dollars to the gentleman for being in our audience tonight." And without knowing it he scuttles his wife's secret project to get him to leave teaching for a job writing radio scripts. Douglas was, of course, channeling Mankiewicz himself, who hated radio and the advertising that paid for its programming. (Television was barely on his radar in 1949: when Paul Douglas' Porter is bragging about his lavishly furnished home he mentions having the only TV in the town; Darnell's Lora Mae sarcastically notes that it doesn't pick up any stations.) The third couple in the film have the most interesting dynamic of all. Lora Mae was once a shopgirl in one of Porter's department stores who set out to snare him with a careful campaign that's recalled in her flashback. The scene begins with their first date, and shows her stringing him along, keeping Porter interested while laying it out plainly that she's only interested in marriage – that she knows their relationship is transactional, and she's holding out for the best price.   Paul Douglas plays Porter as a self-loathing but rich oaf – richer than Brad and his inherited money. He doesn't flatter himself that a woman with Lora Mae's looks is in his league, though her poor background – she literally lives right on the wrong side of the tracks, where passing trains shake the family house – is a leveller. His ideal is Addie Ross, who he tells Lora Mae has "class", and he has her picture in a silver frame in his bookless library. Darnell lets us know that Lora Mae is keenly intelligent, but she isn't above crude ploys like putting runs in her stockings so she can show off her legs to Porter when she senses that his interest is waning as she strings him along. Their marriage is a business deal, made unsentimentally, though the big twist at the end of the picture is that Lora Mae has actually fallen for the big lug, who can't conceive of such an improbability. Audiences will wonder how Lora Mae and Porter fell into the same social circle as Brad, Rita and George, and if you were generous you could imagine that they attended the same local high school in the democratic spirit of American classlessness. A more palpable connection is provided by Sadie (the great Thelma Ritter), the sarcastic maid and cook employed by women like Rita. She's best friend with Lora Mae's mother (Barbara Lawrence) and can be found drinking beer in their kitchen while passing trains threaten to rattle the place apart.   Linda Darnell was in the second phase of her career when she made A Letter to Three Wives. The first began when she was a teenager, scouted by Fox and put under contract, making her first film, Hotel for Women (alongside Sothern) when she was only fifteen years old (and the studio claimed she was nineteen). She played virginal young women and innocent brides in pictures like Day-Time Wife, Brigham Young, The Mark of Zorro and Blood and Sand before transitioning gradually to sultrier adult parts in Summer Storm, Hangover Square and Fallen Angel. She played Wyatt Earp's tempestuous Mexican girlfriend in My Darling Clementine, an ambitious courtesan in Forever Amber and the object of Rex Harrison's homicidal attentions in Preston Sturges' Unfaithfully Yours. Cursed with an overbearing stage mother, Darnell contended with all the sort of attention her looks invited, and while she was married (to cameraman Pev Marley, 23 years her senior) when she made A Letter to Three Wives, Mankiewicz (also married) fell in love with her during shooting. They began an affair that lasted six years; it ended when Mankiewicz wrote The Barefoot Contessa – she assumed the title role was meant for her and felt betrayed when it was given to Ava Gardner. She'd make bad decisions and suffer some bad luck. Her career decline would be painful, her end tragic.   Darnell would work with the great melodrama director Douglas Sirk on pictures like Summer Storm and The Lady Pays Off and it's easy to imagine a story like A Letter to Three Wives in the classic style Sirk would develop later, at the peak of his career. Its plot has similarities to a Sirk classic like All That Heaven Allows, right down to the prosperous suburban setting. In a few years a picture like A Letter to Three Wives would be shot in Technicolor and its beautifully costumed female stars would float through the CinemaScope or VistaVision frame in bright, shadowless wide shots – think of pictures like Designing Woman or The Best of Everything. It would be a very different picture from the one Mankiewicz made, where the cast moves through intimate spaces and two shots. It's actually a funny picture – the trailer makes a point of selling the comedy – full of the kind of wry dialogue Mankiewicz liked and broad scenes like the rumbling Feeney home and Crain's woozy, drunken turn on the country club dance floor in her disintegrating dress. And there's that scene at the dinner party where Mrs. Manleigh theorizes about Sadie's distracted, all-day radio listening. "Sadie may not realize it," she says, "but whether or not she thinks she's listening, she's being penetrated." You can't help but wonder how this clanging double entendre made it past the production code. "After penetration comes saturation," Mrs. Manleigh continues, "and when she's saturated, she'll find herself recommending products to her employers." "Not Sadie," Lora Mae smirks. "I've seen her when she was saturated to the eyes."   A Letter to Three Wives was a box office success, as Zanuck feared. "I can't get along with him now, after four flops," he complained to Sol Siegel about Mankiewicz before giving him the picture. "If he gets a hit with this, he'll be unlivable." Not only was the picture a hit, it got three Oscar nominations including best picture, and won for best adapted screenplay and best director. The story made a big impression on the subcontinent and since 1967 it's been remade in Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, Kannada and Malayalam. In 1985 NBC aired a remake starring Lori Anderson, Michelle Lee, Stephanie Zimbalist and Ben Gazzara, with Ann Sothern in a cameo. It inspired the plot of a Simpsons episode, "Moe Letter Blues". And yet the film sits deep in the shadow of All About Eve, the film Mankiewicz made a year later. It's hard to understand why – they're both stories about a fraught group of friends set against each other by an intimate antagonist. Their settings – middle class suburbia and the theatre – are adult domains that offer little in the way of solace to the afflicted characters. And they both have that barbed, hyper-articulate Mankiewicz dialogue. Maybe it's because A Letter to Three Wives doesn't make its female protagonists heroic; if they enjoy any triumph at the end, it's not over the men in their lives but in fighting off a sneak attack by one of their own.
